# Midpoint components of affine rank at most two are closed
inequality. It locates exactly the first possible affine rank of the
midpoint-component obstruction exhibited in
`candidate 9c01ebb4cdbee199`.

## Theorem

Let P be a finite nonempty complete lattice base in Z^n, meaning

    P=conv(P) intersect Z^n.

Give P the hyperedges {p,q,(p+q)/2} for all distinct p,q in P of the
same parity. If C is a connected component of this hypergraph and
dim aff(C)<=2, then

    conv(C) intersect Z^n=C.

Thus every midpoint component of a complete planar lattice base is
closed in the original lattice. No coarser-lattice replacement is
needed in this rank range. In rank three the preceding exact
thirteen-point example disproves the analogous assertion, even when
the component generates the full original lattice.

## 1. Two elementary component facts

First, different components occupy disjoint parity classes. If p and q
had the same parity in different components, completeness would put
(p+q)/2 in P and its hyperedge would join them. In particular each
component is itself closed under all integral midpoints of its points.

Second, if the endpoints of a lattice segment belong to one component,
then every integer point of that segment belongs to that component.
Write the segment points as a+jv, 0<=j<=m, with v primitive. When
m>=2, all consecutive triples

    {a+jv, a+(j+2)v, a+(j+1)v}, 0<=j<=m-2,

are hyperedges, and their overlapping chain is connected. The cases
m=0 or m=1 have no additional points to prove. Completeness supplies
all these segment points. This proves the theorem already in affine
ranks zero and one.

We will also use the following immediate observation. A finite
midpoint-closed set contained in one parity class is a singleton.
Otherwise take a distinct pair of minimum Euclidean distance. Its
integral midpoint belongs to the set and has half that positive
distance to an endpoint, a contradiction.

## 2. An empty lattice triangle is unimodular

We give the elementary two-dimensional fact needed below, so no lattice
polygon classification or area formula is being invoked. Suppose a
triangle with integer vertices has no lattice points other than its
three vertices. Translate one vertex to zero and call the others a,b.
The vector a is primitive, since otherwise the edge [0,a] would contain
an additional lattice point. Bezout's identity extends a to an integer
basis, so an invertible integer linear change of coordinates sends
a to (1,0). Reflect a coordinate if necessary and write b=(s,t) with
t>0 an integer.

If t>=2, the triangle's section at height one is the interval

    s/t <= x <= (s+t-1)/t.

It contains the integer ceil(s/t): write s=kt+r, 0<=r<t; when r=0 the
left endpoint is integral, and when r>=1 the right endpoint is at
least k+1. Thus (ceil(s/t),1) is an additional lattice point, which is
impossible. Hence t=1. Equivalently, the absolute determinant of the
two edge vectors is one.

## 3. Classification of an isolated interior lattice point

**Lemma.** Let R be a two-dimensional lattice polygon and let
T=R intersect Z^2. If q is an interior point of R and an isolated
vertex of the midpoint hypergraph on T, then an affine unimodular
change of coordinates sends q to zero and T exactly to

    {0, (1,0), (0,1), (-1,-1)}.

**Proof.** Translate q to zero. Isolation implies that zero is not the
midpoint of two distinct lattice points in R. More generally zero
cannot lie in the relative interior of any segment with distinct
integer endpoints in R: the two nearest lattice points to zero along
that segment, one on each side, would have midpoint zero.

Since zero lies in the interior of the polygon, it lies in a triangle
with vertices in T. For example triangulate the polygon using its
integer vertices. It cannot lie on one of the triangulation edges by
the preceding paragraph, so it lies strictly inside one triangle.
Among all integer-vertex triangles in R strictly containing zero,
choose one of minimum positive area; the choice exists because T is
finite. Denote its vertices by a,b,c in counterclockwise order.

That triangle has no integer point other than a,b,c,0. To see this,
an additional point in its interior subdivides it into three strictly
smaller triangles, while an additional nonvertex edge point subdivides
it into two strictly smaller triangles. In either case zero either
lies in the interior of one smaller triangle, contradicting minimality,
or lies on a new segment with integer endpoints, contradicting the
previous paragraph.

The three triangles (0,a,b), (0,b,c), and (0,c,a) are therefore empty
lattice triangles. Section 2 gives

    det(a,b)=det(b,c)=det(c,a)=1.

Use the unimodular basis a,b as coordinates. Then a=(1,0), b=(0,1),
and the latter two determinant identities give c=(-1,-1).

It remains to exclude additional points of T outside this triangle.
Every permutation of its three vertices is induced by an invertible
integer linear map fixing zero. Indeed any two of the vertices form
an integer basis and their sum is the negative of the third. For an
additional integer point p, permute the vertices so that its barycentric
coordinates satisfy alpha>=beta>=gamma, with gamma assigned to
c=(-1,-1). In the new integer coordinates,

    p=(i,j)=(alpha-gamma,beta-gamma), i>=j>=0.

These coordinates are integers. Since p is different from the four
known lattice points, i+j>=2.

If j>=1, then the integer point (1,1) belongs to conv{a,b,p}, because

    (1,1)=[(j-1)a+(i-1)b+p]/(i+j-1).

All coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one. Therefore both c and
-c=(1,1) belong to T, and their midpoint is zero, contradicting
isolation.

If j=0, then i>=2 and 2a=(2,0) belongs to [a,p]. The distinct points
0 and 2a have the same parity and have midpoint a, again contradicting
isolation. No additional p is possible. This proves the lemma. The
four displayed points have distinct parities, so the resulting
four-point hypergraph indeed has no hyperedges. QED.

## 4. Proof of the planar component theorem

Work first in Z^2, and suppose that C has affine rank two. Put

    R=conv(C), T=R intersect Z^2.

Completeness of P implies T subset P. The old hyperedges within C
remain in T, so C is a connected component of the hypergraph on T
as well: restricting cannot join it to another component, and every
path within C is retained.

The component C occupies at least three parity classes. Otherwise,
choose a minimum-positive-area triangle with its vertices in C. Among
its three vertices two have the same parity. Their midpoint belongs
to C, and replacing one endpoint by that midpoint gives a triangle
of half the original positive area, a contradiction.

Assume T differs from C. By disjointness of component parity classes,
all points of T outside C lie in at most one remaining parity class
(there are only four in Z^2). Their set is midpoint-closed: the
midpoint of two such points cannot belong to C, since its hyperedge
would join the components. The singleton observation of Section 1
therefore gives

    T=C union {q}

for one isolated point q. Here C necessarily occupies exactly three
parity classes.

Every lattice point on the boundary of R belongs to C. Indeed each
boundary edge has its endpoints among the extreme points of conv(C),
which belong to C, and Section 1 fills every integer point on that
edge. Thus q is interior to R.

The isolated-interior-point lemma now makes T, up to an affine
unimodular map, exactly {0,e1,e2,-e1-e2}, with q=0. Its other three
points have pairwise distinct parities, so they have no midpoint
hyperedge and cannot form a connected component C. This contradiction
proves T=C and completes the planar case.

## 5. Affine rank two in a higher-dimensional ambient lattice

For a component C of affine rank two in Z^n, choose c in C and put

    V=span_R(C-c), Lambda=V intersect Z^n.

Because V is spanned by integer vectors, Lambda is a rank-two lattice
and an integer basis identifies c+Lambda with Z^2. Also

    aff(C) intersect Z^n=c+Lambda.

This identification preserves all segments, convex combinations, and
integral midpoint relations. In particular two points of c+Lambda
have the same ambient parity if and only if their difference belongs
to 2Lambda: if half their difference is an ambient integer vector, it
also lies in V and hence in Lambda. Thus the finite complete base
conv(C) intersect Z^n and its midpoint components become exactly the
planar objects of Section 4. That result proves closure in the
original ambient lattice as claimed.

The argument concerns lattice points only and does not apply an
untracked coordinate transformation to mixed Hausdorff measure.

## Scope

This proves a genuine low-rank completeness statement and explains why
planar searches did not expose the obstruction. It does not restore
the proposed arbitrary-rank midpoint-component reduction: the exact
rank-three counterexample already has full difference lattice and
cannot be repaired by saturation or a change of affine lattice. No
halfspace-depth lower bound follows from the planar theorem alone.
